transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. How can I help you today?

Hi… yeah, um, I guess the main thing that finally made me come in is work meetings. I’m in advertising sales, and during these long sales strategy meetings I just keep getting up when I know I’m supposed to stay seated. Like I’ll tell myself I’m just refilling my water, or I’ll wander over by the printer for a second, but honestly sometimes I’m just pacing.

And it’s awkward because everyone else is sitting there going through numbers and plans, and I’m trying to look like I’m doing something normal, but I know it’s noticeable. That’s kind of what pushed me to make the appointment.
Do you also find yourself needing to move or having trouble staying seated in other situations, like at home or in social settings?

Yeah, um… the clearest place is definitely work. Like those long sales strategy meetings are honestly what made me finally come in, because I keep getting up when I know I’m supposed to just stay seated. I’ll make it look like I’m refilling my water or checking something by the printer, but sometimes I’m really just kind of pacing.

At home or socially… I mean, I don’t know, I guess I haven’t paid as much attention to it there. Work is where it feels the most noticeable and embarrassing, because everyone else is just sitting there.
Outside of work, like when you're at home relaxing or with friends, do you ever feel restless or have trouble staying seated?

Um… outside of work, I’m not sure I notice it as much. Like, if I’m with friends, there’s usually stuff going on, or we’re at dinner and someone’s telling a story and then I’m thinking about the menu or the lighting or—sorry.

The thing I really keep coming back to is work, because that’s where it’s obvious. In those long sales strategy meetings, I just keep getting up even though I know I’m supposed to stay seated. I’ll make an excuse like getting water, or I’ll drift over by the printer, but sometimes I’m basically just pacing. It feels embarrassing because I know people can see it.
When you're at home relaxing, watching TV or reading, do you ever find yourself getting up frequently or feeling restless, even if it's not in a work setting?

At home… I mean, maybe sometimes, but it’s not the thing I’ve really noticed, if that makes sense. Like if the TV’s on I’ll get up for snacks or move laundry around, and then suddenly I’m reorganizing the mail, but—sorry, that’s probably not what you asked.

The thing that really made me come in is still those long sales strategy meetings. I know I’m supposed to stay seated, and I still keep getting up, like to refill water or just kind of pacing by the printer. That’s where it feels obvious and embarrassing.
When you're at home and not doing anything specific, like when you're watching TV or trying to relax on the couch, do you find it hard to sit still or feel like you need to be moving?

I guess on the couch I’ll get up here and there, but I don’t know if I’d call it the same thing. Like, sometimes the TV’s just background noise and I’m up getting water or checking something, and then I forget what I was watching.

But honestly, the thing that really made me come in is the work meetings. Those long sales strategy meetings—I know I’m supposed to just sit there, and I still end up getting up to refill water or kind of wander by the printer, like I’m making it look purposeful. That’s the part that feels embarrassing.
When you're at home and not in a meeting—like when you're relaxing or watching something you enjoy—do you ever feel like you can't settle down or stay in one place for very long?

Yeah, at home I can be a little up and down, but I keep getting stuck on the work example because that’s the one that feels really obvious. Like in those long sales strategy meetings, I know I’m supposed to stay seated, and I still keep getting up—refilling water, or kind of pacing by the printer like I have a reason to be there. It’s not even like I’m trying to be disruptive, I just… don’t stay put.
When you're at home and engaged in leisure activities, like watching a show or reading, do you often feel restless or have a strong urge to get up and move around?

I mean, at home I do get up sometimes, but I’m not sure I’d say it’s this intense urge exactly. I’ll start watching something and then suddenly I’m in the kitchen or moving something around, but—sorry, I know you’re asking about home.

Honestly, the main thing I keep thinking of is those long sales strategy meetings at work. That’s what made me come in. I know I’m supposed to stay seated, and I still keep getting up, like to refill my water or sort of pace by the printer so it looks like I’m doing something. It’s embarrassing because I know it’s obvious.
When you're in those meetings or trying to focus on something, do you find it hard to pay attention or get distracted easily, even if you're trying to stay focused?

Yeah, definitely. I’ll start out trying to pay attention, like in a longer strategy meeting, and then a few minutes later I realize I’m just staring at the same slide and I don’t actually know what they just said.

It happens with client briefs too. I’ll be reading a paragraph and then somehow I’m still on the same paragraph, but my brain has gone somewhere else—like thinking about a totally different account, or whether I replied to an email, and then I have to go back and reread it. It’s frustrating because I am trying to focus, it’s not like I don’t care.
Looking back, were you someone who had a lot of trouble staying still or sitting quietly during school or other activities when you were a child?

Yeah, I think so. I mean, I don’t remember every detail from being little, but this was definitely before high school. My mom kept some of my elementary school report cards, and the comments were always kind of the same—like, “bright, but rushes,” or that I talked out of turn.

And I had this desk that was just… a disaster. Half-finished worksheets shoved everywhere, homework I forgot to turn in even when I’d done it. I remember being more focused on, like, whether my pencil case had all the colors lined up than on the actual assignment—sorry, that’s probably not the point. But yes, the school comments started pretty early.
When you're at home and trying to relax, like watching a show or reading, do you often feel restless or have a strong urge to get up and move around?

At home it’s a little harder for me to judge, because I’ll tell myself I’m just getting a snack or checking something. But the clearest example is still those long sales strategy meetings at work. I know I’m supposed to stay in my seat, and I keep finding reasons to get up—refill my water, walk over near the printer, that kind of thing. It’s like I need to move, even when I know it probably looks obvious.
Outside of work, in your personal relationships or other activities, have you noticed that this restlessness or difficulty focusing affects how you interact with others or follow through on things?

Yeah… I mean, outside of work I think it probably does, but the place I’ve really noticed it is work. Which I know you asked outside work—sorry. It’s just, that’s where the consequences feel clearest.

It’s started showing up in performance reviews, like comments about follow-through or needing to be more consistent. And there was one client complaint that really got to me. I don’t even remember the exact wording now, but the feeling was like, oh my god, they don’t trust me to stay on top of things. That scared me because I really do care about doing good work, and I don’t want to damage an account just because I lost track of something or didn’t follow through the way I meant to.
Outside of work, have you noticed that your restlessness or difficulty focusing causes problems in your personal relationships, school-related tasks, or other daily activities?

I’m not totally sure, honestly. I don’t have a clean example outside of work that I can point to and say, “yes, that’s definitely it.”

Like, with personal stuff, sometimes I’ll wonder if I’m being a little scattered, but then I also think—doesn’t everyone feel that way? And with school, I mean, I’m not in school now, so it’s hard to compare. I can kind of spiral trying to figure out what counts, because then I start thinking about chores or errands or texting people back, and whether that’s focus or just being busy… sorry, I’m getting off track.

So I guess the honest answer is: I’m not sure I’ve noticed clear problems outside of work.
